I run into the same problem with identifications from around the world on iNaturalist. The app is wrong about 50% of the time on those, too.

I see A LOT of rave reviews about how accurate this is. It makes me wonder how other reviewers are so certain it’s accurate. My guess is that the insect looks something like the Picture Insect photo, and therefore, it must be accurate. 

I’m not sure, but I suspect this app takes the entered photo and compares it to other photos and once it finds something similar, it identifies it. There doesn’t seem to be any consideration about where the insect was located, the habitat, its posture, etc. I had one his morning where it misidentified a transverse ladybug for a seven spotted ladybug.

I could be mistaken, but when I try to correct a misidentification, it only corrects it on my ID. I don’t think it lets the developers know that the app is wrong.

If I don’t trust the app, it doesn’t do me any good. There are much better resources available online.

Is it mildly toxic or can it cause severe allergic reactions? Who knows! The app certainly can’t tell you. 
With gen AI, you get a lot of misinformation fed to the algorithm and it ends up mixed in with the real stuff when the entries are generated. It is negligent to include info at all if you won’t do the bare minimum of looking it over yourself for blatant contradictions. 

It’s definitely a great starting off point for getting an ID, but do your own research afterwards if you want your knowledge to be accurate.

Very useful- some recommendations. Hello, this is my first time writing a review for an app, and the only one I plan on writing until I change my mind again. I have a few points I’d like to go over. 

The app itself functions well. I’m not entirely sure of the inner workings as I’m not a tech guy but it seems to me the more people use and identify bugs it grows the database and becomes more accurate over time. I’ve used this app for 2-3 years on a few different accounts, there’s been a noticeable improvement in terms of precision over that time period. I guess that’s probably an AI thing but I don’t know anything about that. 

That’s my best guess but even if I’m wrong, the function of the app works pretty well. 90-95% successful id, confirmed with a quick google check. At least in my experience with it, but I’m not an Entomologist so in some instances the app and I may be wrong. Pretty reliable in terms of ID. 

My one suggestion would be it seems that sometimes the algorithm gets too focused on a specific part of the bug, instead of the bug as a whole, and produces a crazy range of options. Like from species of wolf spider to butterfly or something along those lines. It’ll see a spider leg as an antennae and then it seems to focus in on the “existence” of an antennae instead of comparing it to the rest of the insect shape. Not sure what the fix may be here, perhaps the order in which it identifies body parts? Infrequent but confusing and slightly frustrating when it happens. 

My bigger issue- the information. The printed texts and fun facts and what not on the insect page will sometimes be wildly inconsistent, even from paragraph to paragraph. The writing structure seems to indicate to me that the information is also written/compiled by AI, and this one does not so well.

 For example on the Spined micrathena page, the description segment claims the spider has no venom. Yet further below, there is a toxicity warning as it claims the spider has a mild venom. Examples like this happen often enough that I really don’t trust the info listed on the page. 

On the same note, some of the descriptions for these bugs seems like a high school English assignment. While I appreciate a good description as the next guy, have the AI turn down the drama like, 30-40%. It’s often difficult to even try to take the listed info seriously when it’s breaking into metaphors and similes about the beauty of the wing design or whatever it may be. Example from the Common pirate spider page follows:

“Suspended in a delicately woven snare, Common pirate spider is a masterful mimic within its habitat, performing an intricate dance of deception and predation. Cloaked in colors that blend seamlessly with the surrounding vegetation, it specializes in capturing not only insects but other spiders, disguising itself and its web to ambush unsuspecting victims. This arachnid has refined this art of imitation to such an extent that its very presence in the ecological tapestry remains a subtle, yet vital stitch.”

Too much, by the ever-lasting, forward march of time that is the length of a singular 
Imperial mile. 

Not to be cynical, but it is a bit silly. 

The app could be an extremely useful scientific/exploratory tool, but in this regard it doesn’t seem to take itself too seriously. 

Overall, good tool, and good identifier. Needs some work with the accuracy and presentation style of the listed information.
